generation.explanation: In flat (Euclidean) geometry this follows from the parallel postulate. Draw a line through one vertex parallel to the opposite side: the two far angles reappear at that vertex as alternate interior angles, and together with the triangle's own angle there they exactly tile a straight line — 180°. Equivalently, the exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°, so the interior angles of a triangle sum to 3×180° − 360° = 180°. Drag the vertices below: no matter how you deform the triangle, the three angles always fit together along the parallel line. (Fun fact: on curved surfaces this fails — spherical triangles have angle sums greater than 180°!)
